name: Charles de Gaulle
description: French leader who founded the Fifth Republic and pursued national independence and state-guided modernisation.
scope: Public positions and conduct during the specified period; this represents the individual rather than all party members or citizens.

axes.brief: Elections and referendums legitimised a strong constitutional presidency.
axes.counter: Emergency powers and executive predominance qualified parliamentary restraint.

axes.brief: Security and public order were strongly defended amid war and unrest.
axes.counter: Electoral opposition and civil institutions persisted alongside coercive powers.

axes.brief: French national unity and integration took precedence over separate communal identity.
axes.counter: Decolonisation acknowledged independent peoples rather than unlimited domestic cultural pluralism.

axes.brief: Labour migration operated within nationally controlled settlement rules.
axes.counter: Views about French identity do not prove each modern numerical or refugee restriction.

axes.brief: Nuclear deterrence and independent defence supported national standing.
axes.counter: Algerian settlement and diplomacy moderated continued military conflict.

axes.brief: National sovereignty and withdrawal from NATO’s integrated command limited supranational control.
axes.counter: France stayed in NATO and European economic cooperation.

axes.brief: Public strategic enterprises and infrastructure coexisted with private business.
axes.counter: State-guided modernisation did not mean nationalising all commerce.

axes.brief: European common-market participation coexisted with strategic national protection.
axes.counter: Sovereign politics are separate from willingness to trade internationally.

axes.brief: Indicative planning and state-directed investment coordinated development.
axes.counter: Most market production was not determined through compulsory output schedules.

axes.brief: Social protection and worker participation accompanied growth and financial stabilisation.
axes.counter: Modern wealth transfers and universal income equalisation are not established.

axes.brief: Secular republican civil institutions coexisted with Catholic tradition and school support.
axes.counter: Personal Catholic belief did not supply a formal clergy veto.

axes.brief: Conventional family and social order coexisted with selective institutional reform.
axes.counter: The contraception-law reform illustrates limits to uniformly traditional estimates.

axes.brief: Nuclear, aerospace and transport modernisation were major development priorities.
axes.counter: Modern biomedical enhancement policy has no direct counterpart.

axes.brief: The national presidency and state administration strongly centralised authority.
axes.counter: The rejected 1969 regional reform demonstrates some willingness to reorganise decentralisation.

axes.brief: National character and education supplied cultural explanations alongside conventional assumptions.
axes.counter: National identity and traditionalism are not a specific genetic theory.
axes.gap: The causal questions are low-confidence historical analogies and must not be treated as documented hereditarian positions.
